description:
SHIPPED s473v (2026-09-16), member 2(a) of perf round 33.  Runtime-only except
for one forward-declaration rule in the compiler (see THE COMPILER HALF).

=== WHAT IT IS ===
A successful match used to WRITE every match variable there is.  It now writes
$1..$20 and a RECORD; the other seven â $+, $^N, %+, %-, @-, @+ and
@{^CAPTURE} â are built from that record the first time one of them is READ.

That is the #477 rule ($&, $`, $' are cut on demand) applied to the rest of
the family, and it is perl's own model: the offsets live in the regexp and the
variables are magic.

WHY $1..$20 STAY EAGER: they are the ones programs actually read, the emitter
reads them as bare symbols, and a capture that IS read pays the same one
subseq either way.  The seven above are the ones almost nobody reads.

=== THE MEASUREMENT THAT CHOSE IT (task #1803) ===
sb-sprof, self time, on THIS tree before the change:

  regexg  (14 M matches of /./g, ZERO capture groups)   trio = 33.6 %
  subste  (one group, only $1 read)                     trio = ~33 %
  textproc                                              trio = ~28 %
  json-rt   set-match-vars / set-capture-groups / clear-capture-groups
            DO NOT APPEAR â not one sample in 3152, because JSON::PP's hot
            regexes are FAILED matches and the trio ran only on success.

Allocation, measured exactly (get-bytes-consed at two N): regexg allocated
~0 bytes per match BEFORE the change, which is #680's reused @-/@+ boxes.  So
"a record per match" had to mean reused storage, not a fresh struct.

=== THE SHAPE ===
cl/pcl-runtime.lisp:
 * THE RECORD (beside the #477 offsets): *match-have*, *match-rs*, *match-re*
   (reused simple-vectors â the register offsets are COPIED out of the
   engine's, so a later FAILED attempt cannot corrupt what the program may
   still read), *match-ngroups*, *match-closers*, *match-reg-names*,
   *match-derived*.
 * SEVEN symbol macros over accessors (%p-last-paren, %p-caret-n,
   %p-plus-hash, %p-minus-hash, %p-at-minus, %p-at-plus, %p-at-capture), each
   calling %p-mv-ensure first.  Symbol macros for #477's reason, unchanged: a
   shared magic BOX would make `push @a, $+` alias.  setf functions for all
   seven, because generated code may still name one as an assignment target
   and the emission must COMPILE.
 * %p-derive-match-vars + %p-derive-offsets / -scalars / -capture-values /
   -named: the materialiser, at most once per successful match.
 * %p-match-record: THE one writer on a successful match, replacing the
   clear-capture-groups -> set-capture-groups -> set-match-vars trio at all
   SIX call sites (rule 11).  %p-set-captures writes $1..$20 and clears what a
   previous match set above the count IN ONE PASS, through a new
   %set-caps-upto macro that nests the twenty guards so a 0-group pattern pays
   ONE fixnum test instead of twenty generic `>` calls.
 * @-/@+ ELEMENTS ARE MAGIC CELLS (%p-at-cell), permanent per index.  This is
   the part that makes the laziness correct: perl's elements are magic and a
   saved \$-[0] reads the CURRENT match (probed).  A materialiser that wrote
   VALUES would refresh the boxes only when @- itself is next read, so a ref
   taken earlier would answer from a stale match â that is exactly what the
   first version did, and the probe caught it.  The cells also give perl's
   read-only death on a write through one.
 * do-regex-match: `str` is DECLARED simple-string (the coercion above already
   decided it) â the per-/g-step (length str) was a full call into the generic
   sequence function, ~5 % of regexg â and the two per-ATTEMPT hash-table-count
   + clrhash calls on %+/%- are GONE.
 * %p-array-store-scalar gained a magic-cell arm: an array store of a
   computed-magic box stores its VALUE.  This is #683's fix (`push @lines, $.`
   gave `3 3 3` where perl gives `1 2 3`) and it is what makes `my @c = @-`
   copy values rather than the magic.
 * %p-symref-array / %p-symref-hash consult *computed-magic-getters* first, so
   @{"-"} and %{"+"} reach the derived state (boundp cannot answer for a
   symbol macro â the ${"&"} rule of #477, widened).

=== THE COMPILER HALF (the one non-runtime change) ===
Pl::ExprToCL::runtime_owned_caret_syms() â the CL symbols a `${^NAME}`-shaped
perl variable resolves to when the RUNTIME owns it, derived from
%SPECIAL_VARS, which is already that table.  Pl::Parser2's forward-declaration
scan uses it: the scan sees only emitted TEXT, where `|@{^CAPTURE}|` is
indistinguishable from the `|${^MPE}|` of an unknown caret global, and it was
emitting a file-level `(defvar |@{^CAPTURE}| â¦)`.  That defvar was a harmless
no-op while the name was a defvar; against a SYMBOL MACRO it is
"Cannot proclaim a macro variable special" â a load-time abort of the whole
file.  Guard: the new match-vars-01.t rows exercise @{^CAPTURE} in a
transpiled program, which is what catches it.

=== THE NUMBERS (A/B, one emission, two cores, interleaved best-of-5) ===
BENCH_RT_B = the 2ac855aa runtime; B/A positive = the OLD runtime is slower.
Box shared with a sibling agent; `uptime` 23:54 load 2.23 2.14 2.24.

  bench       perl(s)   pclA(s)   pclB(s)     B/A    A/perl   (was)
  regexg       0.3956    0.5441    0.8432   +55.0%    1.38x   (2.18x)
  subste       0.0603    0.1999    0.2712   +35.7%    3.32x   (4.78x)
  textproc     0.4599    1.1598    1.5284   +31.8%    2.52x   (3.17x)
  json-rt      0.9279    1.6298    1.6225    -0.4%    1.76x   -- predicted
  strcat       0.3193    0.6913    0.6927    +0.2%    control
  sortnum      0.0267    0.0726    0.0750    +3.3%    control
  sortstr      0.0698    0.1200    0.1197    -0.2%    control
  feread       0.5073    0.1290    0.1324    +2.6%    control
  feread2      0.5040    0.1383    0.1375    -0.6%    control
  feread3      0.5154    0.1288    0.1250    -2.9%    control

Controls inside +/-3.3 %; the three movers are 10x that.  json-rt's -0.4 % is
the profile's own prediction (the trio never appeared in it) and is worth as
much as the movers: the table said which rows could move BEFORE the change.

Peak RSS (/usr/bin/time -f %M, same program, two runtimes) is FLAT:
regexg 33028 vs 33216 kB, textproc 91476 vs 91008, subste 86988 vs 87156.

=== SEMANTICS: 15 + 10 + 1 PROBE ROWS vs perl 5.40.3 ===
scratch/s473v/probe/{match-vars,match-vars2,match-vars3,dot683}.pl, compared
with scratch/s473v/probecmp.pl against perl AND a 2ac855aa extraction.

vs perl: only the two PRE-EXISTING #684 block-scoping rows differ (perl
restores the outer match at block exit; PCL does not), unchanged from base.

vs the base tree THREE rows moved, ALL TOWARD PERL:
  * %+ / %- PERSIST across a failed match.  perl does NOT clear them per
    attempt â the runtime comment that said it does was wrong, and probing it
    is what found this.  (PCL used to clrhash both on every attempt: the wrong
    answer AND two hash-table-count calls per match.)
  * a write through $-[0] DIES, as perl's read-only element does; it used to
    be allowed and stick until the next match.
  * #683: `push @lines, $.` records each line number.

=== GUARD ===
Pl/t/match-vars-01.t 39 -> 50 rows (the owning family file; 3 s).  Inverse-
verified on a `git archive 2ac855aa` extraction: rows 40, 44 and 50 FAIL there
(the three fixes) and the other eight PASS there â which is the point of those
eight: they assert the behaviour the laziness must not break (the @-/@+ sizes
of #417, the saved \$-[0] of #680, the copy rule, $+/$^N with a
non-participating group, @{^CAPTURE} truncation, %- buffers, the symref
spellings, and every derived name before any match at all).

=== WHAT WAS MEASURED AND NOT BUILT (#1803's other three levers) ===
(b) a one-entry cache in front of *p-match-pos*: the WHOLE pos traffic on
    regexg is gethash 1.3 % + puthash 1.5 %, so 2.8 % is the ceiling.  Under
    the bar; not built, and recorded so it is not re-derived.
(c) a cached subject coercion: not measurable â every subject in all four rows
    is already simple, and #1187 closed the same question from the other side.
(d) s///'s per-call protocol: the 7.6 % the table found there is cl-ppcre's
    own generic `scan` dispatch, which is #1808, not this.
subject: THE MATCH RECORD: $+, $^N, %+, %-, @-, @+ and @{^CAPTURE} materialise on READ, not at the match (regexg +65 %, subste +34 %, textproc +25 %)
